body.p: present act of Existence. There is a greater similarity to Kant, where “pure reason”, theory is only freeing space, but the steps towards Transcendence are steps of “practical reason”, of freedom.

Let me give a few instances where we will be able to recognize the same central gesture of Jaspers’ thought. In psychiatry: Jaspers requires the utmost careful exploration of possible physiological factors of the disease as well as of the objective physiological facts. But the more careful and complete the picture of these elements is, the more it becomes evident to the psychiatrist that the medical “explanation” (“erklärende Psychologie”) is not sufficient, however necessary, and should not be the only approach. Jaspers listens very carefully to what the patient himself has to say about his subjective experience and he tries “to understand” it in a way completely different from that used in the causal explanations mentioned before. The “understanding psychology” (“verstehende Psychologie”) is not a method by which the causes of the disease are established, but one through which the process described and experienced by the patient, is subjectively “imitated” by oneself. When you say to a friend, “I understand you”, it does not mean that you know the causes of his behaviour, but that you can put yourself in his skin and go subjectively through the same development.

Now, Jaspers shows that neither the “explaining psychology” nor the “understanding psychology” is able to reach a knowledge of any mental disease as a whole: each of these methods, and both together, can only approach different aspects of it, aspects of the sick self. Yet both should remain clearly distinct from each other, so that a plurality of distinct methods is required, none of which has the right to be elusive of the others, as if it could reach the whole. This was the chief criticism Jaspers directed against psychoanalysis: it has a pretense to exclusiveness, taking advantage of a methodical lack of clarity, pretending to be “explanatory” whereas the meaning of the terms it used actually required a subjective “understanding”. We recognize here, in the field of psychiatry, the plurality of approaches, aiming at an unreachable whole, the experience of a necessary failure, and the existential meaning of this failure, which reveals the irreducible self of the patient — beyond all methodical approaches — as a possibility of Existence in its authenticity. Jaspers used to say that even in the worst mental disease an ultimate possibility of Existence cannot be denied and requires absolute respect.

A quite different example: Jaspers’ conception of existential “communication”. This communication could perhaps be less important in times when human beings have a common creed, live in a common order and enjoy common purpose of life. But communication becomes an existential need in a broken world, where traditional values are less and less effective. When the common symbols and sense of transcendence have lost their power, the self of the thinking individual becomes empty, looks upon an empty everyday life which is no real life at all.
